label: Parenting Young Children
framing: The early years are not a delay before the real parenting begins. They are the parenting, the slow patient shaping of a small soul by ten thousand ordinary moments no one will applaud. Scripture frames children as a gift and a charge, given not to be owned but to be raised toward God and then released.
cultural: Our culture both worships children and outsources them, treating these years as a thing to be optimized or survived rather than received. We are told to fear that every misstep scars them, and so we hover and exhaust ourselves. The Bible is steadier, asking not for perfect parents but faithful ones who teach as they walk and sit and rise, in the grain of the ordinary day.
historical: The command to teach the children was given to Israel at the very founding of the people, repeated morning and evening in the Shema for over three thousand years. Susanna Wesley, raising her many children in the early eighteenth century, gave each one an hour of her attention in turn, and from that crowded house came John and Charles Wesley, who shook a nation.
application: Parent for the heart and not only the behavior, since a child managed but not reached will comply now and leave later. Discipline with warmth and not in your own anger, aiming to instruct rather than to vent. Repent to your children when you are wrong, which teaches them grace more than any lecture. And guard your own soul through these tiring years, for you cannot give a peace you are not receiving.

verses.text: In the future, when your son asks, “What is the meaning of the decrees and statutes and ordinances that the LORD our God has commanded you?” then you are to tell him, “We were slaves of Pharaoh in Egypt, but the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand.
verses.where: Moses tells Israel how to answer when a child asks what the commandments mean. The site's note points out that the answer is a story, not a rule: we were slaves, and the LORD brought us out. The question assumes the child has watched the commands being kept at home before asking why.

verses.text: And He took the children in His arms, placed His hands on them, and blessed them.
verses.where: People bring little children for Jesus to bless, and the disciples scold them. Jesus is angry, tells them not to hinder the children, and then takes them in his arms, lays his hands on them and blesses them. Small children were not an interruption to his work.

verses.text: “Truly I tell you,” He said, “unless you change and become like little children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven. Therefore, whoever humbles himself like this little child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven. And whoever welcomes a little child like this in My name welcomes Me.
verses.where: When the disciples argue about greatness, Jesus stands a little child in the middle of them. The note says he turns from becoming like a child to receiving children: whoever welcomes a little one in his name welcomes him. The ordinary work of caring for a small child is, in his words, welcoming Christ.

verses.text: It was I who taught Ephraim to walk, taking them in My arms, but they never realized that it was I who healed them. I led them with cords of kindness, with ropes of love; I lifted the yoke from their necks and bent down to feed them.
verses.where: God remembers Israel's childhood in the language of a parent: he taught the child to walk, took it in his arms, bent down to feed it. The same chapter grieves that the child ran from him. Scripture's picture of God as a parent includes the patient, physical, unseen work of the earliest years.

verses.text: As a mother comforts her son, so will I comfort you, and you will be consoled over Jerusalem.”
verses.where: In the book's last chapter God promises to comfort his people as a mother comforts her son, carrying them and bouncing them on her knees. The prophet reaches for the most ordinary scene of early childhood to describe God's own tenderness. A parent comforting a small child is doing something God himself does.

verses.text: When I was a son to my father, tender and the only child of my mother, he taught me and said, “Let your heart lay hold of my words; keep my commands and you will live.
verses.where: The father passes on what his own father taught him when he was small. Wisdom in Proverbs moves down the generations by being spoken at home, by someone who first received it himself. A parent teaches young children best what he is still learning.

verses.text: I am reminded of your sincere faith, which first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice, and I am convinced is in you as well.
verses.where: Writing from prison, Paul remembers that Timothy's sincere faith lived first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice. Elsewhere Paul says Timothy knew the Scriptures from infancy (3:15). The faith of a young pastor had been passed on in an ordinary home by a mother and a grandmother.

verses.text: I prayed for this boy, and since the LORD has granted me what I asked of Him, I now dedicate the boy to the LORD. For as long as he lives, he is dedicated to the LORD.” So they worshiped the LORD there.
verses.where: Hannah, who had prayed for a son through years of grief, brings the young Samuel to the sanctuary and gives him to the LORD. The site's note says the chapter does not command parents to do what she did, and that it was not easy; she visited him every year and made him clothes. It describes a mother giving back to God the gift she most wanted.

verses.text: “Go and lie down,” he said to Samuel, “and if He calls you, say, ‘Speak, LORD, for Your servant is listening.’” So Samuel went and lay down in his place.
verses.where: The boy Samuel hears his name in the night and runs three times to Eli, until the old priest understands and teaches him how to answer God. Eli had failed with his own sons, and still he helped this child learn to listen. The first lesson in faith is often a sentence an adult gives a child to say.

verses.text: And Jesus grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man.
verses.where: After the visit to the temple at twelve, Jesus goes home and lives obediently with Mary and Joseph, and grows in wisdom and stature. The site's note says that as a human being he really learned and really had a childhood. The Son of God was raised by parents, one ordinary year after another.

misread.taken: Parents of young children often hear this verse as a formula: get these early years right, with the right devotions and the right discipline, and the child is guaranteed to stay in the faith. It turns ordinary parenting into an anxious test that can be failed.
misread.says: The site's note on the chapter says a proverb describes how life usually goes: early training tends to shape a whole life. It is a true and encouraging generalization, not a contract, and Proverbs itself keeps warning well-taught children not to leave what they were taught. Interpreters differ on what the way he should go means, whether the way of wisdom or training suited to the child's own character. On any reading the verse urges parents to take the task seriously; it does not make them the sole cause of their children's faith.
misread.text: Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it.

whole: The years with small children are full and tiring and strangely invisible. The days are long and the work repeats: meals, baths, spills, the same question asked forty times, a night broken three times. Many parents feel they are failing at everything at once, or that their real life and their spiritual life have both been put on hold. Christian parents often add a quieter worry, that they are not doing enough devotions or prayers or teaching, and that the child's whole future depends on getting this stage right.

Scripture sees these years more steadily. It takes them seriously, because the first teaching of faith in Israel happened at home, in answer to a child's question, in the middle of ordinary life. And it refuses to make them a performance. God describes himself as the parent who taught a child to walk and bent down to feed it, the mother who comforts a son on her knee. Jesus took small children in his arms when his disciples thought they were in the way. The Son of God himself spent years growing up in a home. Small children are not an interruption to the life of faith; for a season, they are much of it. The anxiety comes when we forget that a child is a person before God, not a project whose outcome rests on us.

So the wisdom here is humble and steady. Tell the story of what God has done, the way Israel's parents did, more than you recite rules. Let children see faith practiced before they understand it, because the question of what it means comes from watching. Bless them; touch them; comfort them; welcome them as Jesus did. Teach them a sentence of prayer the way Eli taught Samuel, even on the days you are not sure of your own. Ask for help: Timothy's faith came through a grandmother as well as a mother, and the church is meant to share this work. And forgive yourself the ordinary failures, the short temper and the missed bedtime prayer, because your child will learn grace partly by watching you receive it.

Underneath it all is the God who formed each child and will not lose track of them. Hannah gave her son back to the LORD, and every parent does the same in smaller ways every day. The faith of a child is finally God's gift, not a parent's achievement, and that is not a reason to do less. It is the freedom to do the next small thing faithfully, without the weight of having to guarantee the ending.

differ.share: Christians agree that children are a gift from God and bear his image, that Jesus welcomes them, that parents are called to teach them the faith at home, and that the whole church shares the work of raising them.

views.name: Baptized as infants
views.body: Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, Methodist and Reformed churches baptize the infants of believers as members of the covenant community. The site's note on Colossians 2 records that some see baptism as the new covenant sign parallel to circumcision, and the note on Mark 10 that Luther's baptismal order and the 1549 Book of Common Prayer read Jesus' blessing of the children at infant baptism.

views.name: Dedicated, then baptized on profession of faith
views.body: Baptist and many other churches dedicate infants with prayer and baptize on a person's own profession of faith. The same note on Colossians 2 records that they point to being raised through faith (verse 12) and so baptize believers.

differ.after: Both bring their children to Jesus to be blessed, and both pray for the day the child's faith is their own.

deep.sit: What is one story of what God has done, in Scripture or in your own family, that your child could hear from you this week, in your own words, at an ordinary moment?

prayer.lead: Three verses for a tired parent, about a soul quieted like a weaned child resting with its mother.
prayer.text: My heart is not proud, O LORD, my eyes are not haughty. I do not aspire to great things or matters too lofty for me. Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul; like a weaned child with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me. O Israel, put your hope in the LORD, both now and forevermore.
